- Verification (reading) and documentation (writing) are asymmetric. After verifying items complete, explicit write-back is required to prevent stale state. Applies to sprint checklists, MEMORY.md stale claims, last-align.txt markers.
- Scale-test output-size designs before coding. A 3-file TDD fixture passed 22 tests, but generate_hierarchy (list-all-files-and-sections) would emit ~4,700 lines on the real 4,703-node DSM Central target; the toy fixture certified an unbounded-output bug as healthy. When output size is itself a design parameter, include a scale-representative case or compute projected size for the real target before implementing, so unbounded designs fail at design time, not after green tests.

## S48 (2026-04-20)

- Dedicated small sprint beats mixed sprint when boundary clarity matters. Sprint 17 = TOON migration alone (1-1.5 sessions) preserves DEC-010 C3 validation gate as a clean boundary. Sprint size is not the sole criterion; boundary clarity is.
- "proceed" is not a protocol waiver. The agent rationalized a bare "proceed" at session start into skipping the collaboration gates and was interrupted ("also stop for the collaboration gates"). "proceed" authorizes the next step under the active protocol; when no gate has yet been established this session, default to presenting Gate 1, not to momentum.
- Decide-vs-implement reframe. For a large recommendation (TOON migration, ~1 session of code), the correct session output was a decision artifact (DEC-010 + scoped BL), not code. When a request could be read as "do the work," first check whether the right output is a decision + scoped BL; separate deciding from implementing.
- Protocol corrections are session-scoped, not turn-scoped. After the gate correction on Item 1, Items 2-3 ran a clean Gate1-2-3 rhythm with no re-prompting. Propagate a mid-session protocol correction to all remaining work units without waiting to be told again.

## S49 (2026-04-23 / resumed 2026-06-09)

- Mark resumption gaps explicitly in the transcript. When /dsm-go Steps 5.5/6 (archive+reset) are deliberately skipped to preserve in-flight gate context, the transcript spans the gap with mixed dates/models (opus-4-7 April → opus-4-8 June); an explicit boundary marker prevents it being misread as continuous.
- Process-audit questions are honesty triggers. When the user asks how/why a protocol step was performed, audit your actual tool calls against the spec and disclose deviations; do not restate the spec as if you followed it. S49 saw three probes ("how did the version check work?", "where was MEMORY read from?", "why is the transcript still S49?"), each exposing an unmarked shortcut. Pre-empt by stating shortcuts when you take them.
- Name the cost and the spec-faithful alternative when deliberately deviating from a protocol step. Skipping /dsm-go Steps 5.5/6 to preserve gate context was logged at decision time with its cost (a 6-week mixed-provenance transcript) and the alternative (archive+reset), so when the user challenged it later the tradeoff was already on record.
- Protocol-mandated is not the same as automatic. When a mandated action is both context-expensive and triggered in an anomalous situation (e.g. /dsm-align on an 8-version drift mid-resumption of an unwrapped session), surface the decision to the user rather than auto-running it.
- Split parallel research agents by adversarial angle (survey vs critique vs fit), not into redundant surveys, then drive the recommendation with the convergence plus the single decisive datum, not an average. S49 GraphRAG used 3 Sonnet agents; the decisive fact was "Leiden clustering is already on the Sprint 18 roadmap", so adopt-ideas-only followed without needing GraphRAG itself.
- An interrupting question consumes no gate. When a presented-but-unapproved concept gate is interrupted by an unrelated question, re-confirm that gate after resolving the interruption; do not read a later "continue" as approval of it. Also re-present concept gates when resuming after a multi-week conversation gap, since approvals do not survive across conversations.
- A logged lesson does not self-enforce; recurring failure modes need a mechanism. The S48 "close the wrap-up loop in one pass" lesson recurred immediately (S49 sat unwrapped 6 weeks), and what caught it was /dsm-go's branch#>MEMORY# resumption detection, not the lesson. Escalate recurring failure modes to an enforceable check rather than re-logging them.

## S50 (2026-06-25)

- For a large decision artifact, surface the scope fork explicitly rather than picking silently. DEC-011 offered adopt+minimal-experiment-scope (Option A) vs full-architecture commitment (Option B); a non-binding "leanings" table let an Accepted DEC decide the model and defer the schema details in one document, mirroring DEC-009's anti-over-commitment lesson.
- Partial answer to a multi-item prompt — proceed on your recommendation but state the assumption. When the user answers some sub-questions and is silent on the one you flagged as the key decision (S50: "1. accepted, 2. yes" with no word on the A/B scope fork), do not silently assume on the flagged item and do not re-block for an answer they are clearly ready to move past; proceed with the recommended option and state the assumption explicitly so they can correct it. Distinct from surfacing the fork (that is the prior step); this is handling the silence on it.
- S50's wasted cycles were entirely tooling-mechanical, not reasoning — and disclosure lessons transferred cleanly. Near-zero reasoning reversals; every friction point was infrastructure (transcript Edit-anchor failure ×2 → heredoc fallback; `## [v` grep miss). Meanwhile two S49 [STAA] lessons executed un-prompted: "protocol-mandated ≠ automatic" (surfaced the expensive /dsm-align rather than auto-running it) and "state shortcuts proactively" (wrap-up enumerated all skipped steps + the Step 8.5 /humanizer deviation with reasons). Surfacing/disclosure lessons transfer across sessions; the recurring failures are mechanical and need mechanisms (hooks, marker-writing), not re-logged lessons.

## S51 (2026-06-25 / 2026-06-26 light continuation)

- A cheap correlated proxy accepted at verification time can hide a failing real metric for a whole session. P1b spot-checked "TOON 188 lines vs markdown 212 lines" and read fewer lines as progress toward the token-reduction goal, but deferred the ~1-minute C3 token gate to a later phase; S52 then ran that gate and it FAILED (+7.58% GE, fewer chars but MORE BPE tokens). When the success metric is X (tokens) and the proxy you happen to measure is a correlated-but-different Y (lines/chars), run X rather than let Y stand in — especially when the phase plan sequences an expensive irreversible step (golden freeze) ahead of the cheap falsifiable gate. Question freeze-before-gate ordering at the moment you are able to run the gate. Precursor side of S52 #73/#74.
- Reasoning-lessons carry guard conditions; re-evaluate the condition, do not cargo-cult the verdict. S47 #13/#14 said defer the data/format split until "the second format is actually built"; in S51 TOON made the second format concrete, so the agent re-checked the guard, found it satisfied, and applied the split citing the condition — the correct positive inverse of blanket-applying a prior "don't".

## S52 (2026-07-03)

- A capability experiment can double as an adjudicated cross-model review. Design the brief so the reviewing model's findings are verifiable (structured schema, cite file:line), then INDEPENDENTLY REPRODUCE the load-bearing claim rather than accept it. All 14 Fable-5 findings survived Opus adjudication; the one that changed the sprint (the C3 token gate) I re-ran myself and it matched to the token. The adjudication table is the trust boundary that makes a fresh model's output actionable.
- Delegate token-cheap gathering to a cheaper model, reserve the expensive model for analysis. A one-line brief directive ("delegate cheap tasks to lighter models, reserve yourself for the analytical/critical part") produced the intended split: Fable put ~65-70% of ~270-300K tokens on Haiku gatherers and spent its own budget on judgment. Making the wider read-set affordable was what justified going wide.
- Run a falsifiable validation gate EARLY, before the artifact it guards is frozen. DEC-010's C3 token gate was runnable in under a minute and FAILED (+1.74% Central / +7.58% GE vs required −10%). The plan sequenced P2 (golden-fixture freeze) before P3 (the gate); that ordering would have enshrined a schema that cannot ship. Gate-before-freeze whenever the gate has no real dependency on the freeze.
- When an assessment reopens a decision, formalize the finding and the halt but DEFER the direction decision. Annotated DEC-010 (amendment, not a new DEC), recorded the course correction in BL-302, wrote a handoff enumerating the forks — separating "record the reckoning" from "decide the response", so the next session decides with full context instead of the current one deciding under time pressure.
- Content that will seed a downstream agent's reasoning gets source-grounding plus user approval before it anchors. The north-star statement in brief.md would drive Fable's whole strategic-alignment axis, so it was grounded in vision-research and README (not paraphrased from MEMORY) and user-approved before handoff, because an error there propagates into the downstream model's output. Extends Voice-Attribution and vision-grounding to the seeds-another-agent case.
- Use absolute paths in any brief or handoff a separate session or agent will consume. Fable ran in its own session with an unknown cwd, so the read-set and the launch prompt used absolute paths, not repo-relative ones. You cannot assume the consumer's working directory.

## S53 (2026-07-06)

- Gate multi-agent orchestration on a concrete quality gain, not parallelism. The user conditioned Workflow use on "only if results can be better"; the justification was that agent transcripts yield ACCURATE tool-call counts vs unreliable self-report — validated when pilot self-reports matched transcript counts exactly. Choose the heavier harness when it buys measurement fidelity/reproducibility, not just speed.
- A "failed" agent can still hold the correct answer. A pilot subagent hit the StructuredOutput retry cap but had computed the right result (112 orphans) and merely omitted required schema fields; recovered verbatim from its transcript. Inspect failed-agent transcripts before discarding, and relax over-strict schemas to require only the load-bearing field.
- For an A/B on "does artifact X help", design trap + control tasks, not only X-friendly ones. EXP-011 mixed ToC-answerable tasks with an F4 orphan-truncation trap (where the ToC could mislead) and out-of-scope controls (src/ questions the ToC cannot answer); a ToC-only-friendly set would have rigged the result.
- Scope experiment questions to the artifact's coverage boundary at design time. T4 ("largest directory") was not scoped to dsm-docs/, so all three arms answered repo-wide and it failed to discriminate — a wasted cell caught only post-run. Bound each question to what the artifact under test actually covers.
- Pre-register success criteria + the ground-truth answer key BEFORE running, so the decision is mechanical. EXP-011 fixed the >=25% tool-call gate and the key before any agent ran; applying the pre-registered rule to the observed rollup made the NO-GO decision fall out without post-hoc argument.
- When evaluating "is X worth fixing or adopting?", the current defective X is the correct treatment arm, do not fix it first. EXP-011 used the current broken TOON emitter as the TOON arm and refused the 7-item fix list as a prerequisite, because the defects (bloat, F4 orphan truncation) are exactly what the experiment should penalize, so fixing first presupposes the answer and would burn a sprint. Removed a false gating dependency.
- Pilot a representative slice, including the trap case, to validate the harness and instrument before the full spend. Before the 18-run batch a 6-run pilot (T1 plus the T3 orphan-trap, times 3 arms) confirmed transcript tool-counts matched self-report and surfaced an over-strict-schema failure class that was fixed for the batch. Concrete payoff: the schema fix would otherwise have cost 18 agents.
- "Do we have enough to X?" is a readiness assessment, not authorization to do X. Asked whether there was enough to post about the experiment, the agent answered have-vs-gaps (~90%, 6 gaps flagged) and did NOT draft the blog post, routing drafting through its own chunked-drafting Gate 1. Assess-vs-produce, distinct from decide-vs-implement.

## S54 (2026-07-09)

- A protected-branch merge of the agent's own PR needs specific authorization; a generic "proceed in priority order" does not clear it. The auto-mode classifier blocked the self-merge, matching the agent's own pre-committed plan to stop and confirm. Do the safe prep (commit + push), then gate the irreversible publish on an explicit, specific go.
- When asked to file feedback conditional on a principle being missing or ill-framed, verify findability + framing first and refuse to manufacture the item when the condition is not met. S54's inclusive-language rule was both findable (DSM_0.2 §13) and well-framed, so no Central feedback was written.
- In chunked drafting, framing supplied by the user mid-pipeline can be load-bearing for already-locked bites. Before spending the next bite, capture the framing to materials.md, confirm your read, and re-open the prior sections it changes. S54's metric-selection framing arrived after Section 1 was drafted and forced a Section 1 revision. The per-bite pipeline is forward-only by default; backward propagation is manual.
- Gate on the cost of a misread, not on protocol. S54 paused before Section 2 explicitly because the distinction was subtle enough that a wrong read would waste a ~275w draft. When the next step is cheap, proceed and state the assumption instead.
- When a user rejects a specific word, determine whether the objection is lexical or categorical BEFORE substituting. S54 read "no word 'kill'" as lexical, substituted "kill-switch"->"tripwire", and was rejected again when the user stated the real rule (no weapons/military/killing vocabulary). Cost: one wasted round-trip plus a substitution that was worse under the actual rule. On any word-level rejection, infer or ask the category, then sweep the whole document once.
- Before saving a user correction as a novel preference memory, check whether it is an existing methodology rule you failed to apply. S54 filed the inclusive-language rule as a new user preference, then found it was DSM_0.2 §13 (lists "kill", names blog posts in scope) and rewrote the memory as a pointer plus an adherence note. Misfiling inflates the preference store and hides an adherence gap as personal taste.
- Answer terminology questions against the project's own reserved vocabulary before the general definition. "Is the Intrinsic-ToC an ontology?" resolved to no, because the vision doc reserves "ontology" for Layers 3/4/4.5; the general CS definition would have said yes and clashed with the roadmap.
- Number Gate 4 findings and split them SAFE (apply inline) vs OPTIONAL (present for decision). S54's 6 findings drew a 9-word reply; also state your disambiguation of any compressed answer, since "5) keep" was ambiguous between two referents.
- Derive "pending" items from machine markers, not carried-forward prose. S54 listed "STAA for S52" as pending at boot and at close while last-staa.txt read 53 and [STAA] S52 entries were already in the lessons file. Mirror of the S50 marker-absent case; both fail because the prose list and the marker are maintained separately.
- S49's "mark resumption gaps explicitly" recurred: S54 spanned 2026-07-06 to 2026-07-09 with the final Output block stamped 18:22 after a 21:00 User block, no [RETROACTIVE] or gap marker. Recurring transcript-hygiene failures need a hook check (block timestamp vs file mtime), not another logged lesson.

## S55 (2026-07-21)

- A stale LOCAL ref is not evidence about a remote branch. `git log master..session-54` reported "2 commits ahead" and I read that as "unmerged", but the branch had already merged remotely via PR #12; only the local `master` ref was stale. A remote-side PR merge never moves a local ref. Cost: a wrong recommendation the user approved, caught only when `git push` was rejected with "tip is behind". For "is this branch merged", compare against `origin/<main>` or fetch first.
- A forward-justification claim can outlive the decision it justified and misdirect downstream scope. BL-302 line 77 ("Phase 2 requires native nesting; TOON handles this, incumbent does not") was written before any TOON emitter existed to check it against; by the time one did, the claim had done its work and nobody re-read it. It survived the abandonment of TOON and still shaped Sprint 18. When inheriting scope, re-check its PREMISES, not just its status.
- Prefer the seconds-long empirical check over the plausible inference. Two findings this session came from running something rather than reasoning about it: (a) `should_exclude` matches segment-by-segment, so a bare `.venv` pattern matches nothing nested, which would have shipped a DEFAULT_EXCLUDES list that excluded nothing while tests passed; (b) an unrelated-looking test failure was confirmed pre-existing by stashing and running it on clean HEAD. Both inferences would have gone the other way.
- A green test can be green for the wrong reason, so interrogate unexpected passes during the red phase. `test_opt_out_disables_defaults` passed before implementation because Pydantic silently drops unknown kwargs (`extra` defaults to ignore), so the opt-out kwarg vanished and, with nothing yet excluded, the assertion held vacuously. In TDD, an unexpected PASS in the red phase is a defect signal, not good news.
- Edit forward-looking claims contradicted by outcomes; preserve records of what was believed at the time. This asymmetry governed six artifacts: BL-302 line 77 kept its text plus a REFUTED marker, the epoch plan's S47 Q3 "Migrate to TOON" record was left untouched, while the Sprint 17 rationale two sections later was corrected. Same document, opposite treatment, because one is a record and the other is a plan.
- When a change legitimately breaks an existing test, reframe what it asserts AND add a paired test preserving the original contract, rather than loosening the assertion. Two `test_config.py` tests asserted `merged.exclude == ["plan/*"]` exactly; each now checks user patterns stay first, with a new `use_default_excludes=False` test keeping exact equality. Loosening alone would have silently deleted a guarantee.
- `--knowledge-summary` had been emitting dependency content since Sprint 16 (16 of 57 directories from `.venv`/`.pytest_cache`) and nobody noticed, because the defect is only visible in the tool's own output, which is read by agents rather than humans. Output consumed by machines needs periodic human inspection; no test failed and no user complained.
- A success criterion can become unsatisfiable and sit unnoticed inside a definition of done. The epoch-5 plan required the DEC-010 C3 gate to PASS; the gate ran in S52 and failed, so the epoch could never be closed as written. Reframed to "the phase reached a recorded resolution", since a gate that correctly rejects its candidate is a successful gate. Re-read success criteria after any halt or abandonment.
- Prevent staged-rename bundling with explicit pathspec commits rather than flagging it afterwards. The `/dsm-go` Step 3.5 checkpoint rename sat in the index across four commits and entered none of them, because every commit used `git commit -- <paths>`; it landed in the boot commit where it belonged. Directly closes the S51 #63 recurrence, where the same rename rode along twice despite being flagged.
- When user replies compress to one or two words across a whole session, widen the disambiguation channel proportionally: state your read of each reply before acting on it. S55 ran 9 sub-three-word approvals ("your recommendation", "(a) then (b)", "approve t", "go", "ok", "we can continue", "I agree") with zero misreads, because every one was restated first, including a garbled "approve t" read as "approve" plus a stray keystroke. Extends S54 #107 from the single-ambiguous-reply case to the whole-session cadence.
- When a tool rejects an action your model says should succeed, the rejection is evidence against the model, not an obstacle to route around. S55's wrong "session-54 is an unmerged leftover" recommendation, already approved and partly executed, surfaced only because a push rejected with "tip is behind its remote counterpart" was investigated instead of retried. A fetch-then-retry would have succeeded and buried the error.
- `/dsm-go` Step 0c's leftover-branch check compares against the LOCAL main ref with no preceding fetch, so a branch merged remotely via PR reads as carrying unmerged commits. Fetch, or compare against `origin/<main>`, before reporting a leftover. Per S49 #50 this is the mechanism-not-another-lesson case: the "resolve the artifact before assuming its meaning" shape is now on record twice (S50 #55 marker format, S55 #113 ref staleness).
- When committing work that is code-complete but not deliverable-complete, record the outstanding items in the commit message, not only in conversation, since conversation state does not survive the session and the commit does. S55 split P1 into 03f82b8 (code, with the unmet docs MUST named as "Outstanding for this phase") then 5899984 (docs), rather than holding verified green work hostage to prose or letting the debt surface at sprint close.
- A plan authored earlier in the same session binds that session's execution. S55 created the Level 3 branch per the Branch Strategy it had written into the sprint plan two hours earlier, and kept the "phase detail lives in the BL, the sprint plan only points at it" division it had promised one artifact before, verifying the promise at the next artifact. A plan whose first instruction its author ignores is worthless.
- Verify a naming or numbering convention against the target file BEFORE stamping it, not in post-write verification. The same error class fired twice in S55 with opposite outcomes: a `DEC-009-remove-local-llm-dependencies.md` link was invented and caught after the write, while "Amendment 3" was caught before the write when a check showed the numbered-amendment sequence lives on DEC-010 and BL-302 has no numbered amendments at all. The pre-write check costs one read.
- When an approved edit uncovers adjacent stale state, report it as a separate decision rather than folding it into the approved diff, because quietly widening an approved edit is how a diff stops matching what was reviewed. S55 found 6 stale items while making an approved 2-line edit, changed none of them, flagged the one with real consequence (an unsatisfiable success criterion), and got a separate commit authorized for five of the six.
- Merging a Level 3 branch is a PHASE boundary, not a sprint boundary. Fire the Phase Boundary Checklist, keep the sprint open in MEMORY ("IN PROGRESS, P1 complete, P2-P4 pending"), and state the distinction before invoking `/dsm-wrap-up`, so the skill does not record a partial sprint as closed on the strength of Level 3 activity.
- The Sprint Boundary Checklist exists in two divergent forms, 7 items in `.claude/CLAUDE.md` and 9 items in the sprint-17 and sprint-18 plan files. Sprint 18's plan mirrors the 9-item in-repo version, surfaced rather than silently picked. Reconcile before Sprint 18 close, or the `/dsm-go` Step 3.6 gate compares against an ambiguous standard.

## S56 (2026-07-21)

- An attribute appearing in `dir()` is not evidence the capability exists. `networkx.algorithms.community` lists `leiden_communities`, and I was one sentence from recommending "networkx already ships Leiden, no new dependency". Calling it raised `NotImplementedError: ... included in NetworkX as an API to dispatch to other backends`. The listing is the interface; only invocation is the capability. Same family as S55's seconds-long-check lesson, new trigger: introspection output.
- Do not spend an unpriced cost as an argument. I told the user `python-igraph` was "a compiled C extension" and used it as the cost against adopting leidenalg, then priced it when asked to commit: both packages resolve as prebuilt abi3 manylinux wheels, 8.4 MB, no toolchain. The asserted cost had been the main argument against the option and it evaporated on contact. Price a cost before it carries weight in a recommendation.
- A test whose result could not have come out the other way proves nothing. The seed-reproducibility check on igraph's karate club returned "identical across 5 runs at seed 42", which looked like confirmation, but the controls returned 1 distinct partition across 20 DIFFERENT seeds and 1 across 10 UNSEEDED runs. An entirely ignored seed parameter produces exactly that output. Re-run on a graph where the algorithm is genuinely stochastic before believing a determinism claim. Extends S55's green-for-the-wrong-reason lesson from TDD reds to verification generally.
- Pre-register the falsification condition BEFORE the measurement that could kill your own recommendation. I predicted a sharp NMI transition across the CONTAINS weight sweep and wrote down that a flat curve would mean the family is dead. NMI came back flat at 0.755-0.767 across every nonzero weight, and the design died cleanly on a condition I could not renegotiate. Without the pre-registration, flat NMI reads as "no strong signal either way" and the design survives on inertia.
- A quality metric that a randomized null also satisfies was never measuring quality. Low NMI-vs-directories was used all session as evidence that clustering found structure the folder tree does not encode; a degree-preserving rewire scored the same or higher (0.1881 null vs 0.1812 real). It measured the ABSENCE of folder agreement, not the PRESENCE of topical structure. Any gate metric should be validated against a null before it is trusted, not against an absolute threshold.
- Read internal prior art before commissioning external research. The S49 GraphRAG study named DSM Central as the target corpus; I had spent most of the session measuring GE, the tool's own repository. One file read relocated the experiment's target, and no amount of reasoning would have surfaced it. Internal prior art is cheaper than external search and more likely to be decisive.
- When adopting a technique from a system while rejecting that system's machinery, check whether the machinery was load-bearing FOR the technique. S49 adopted GraphRAG's Leiden clustering while rejecting its LLM entity extraction as DEC-009-incompatible, but the extraction is what produces a clusterable substrate: GraphRAG does not cluster document cross-references at all. The algorithm was carried forward and the thing that fed it was left behind. Second instance in this project of a claim outliving its context (S55 BL-302 line 77 was the first).
- State your own base rate when it is bad. After two wrong recommendations on the same decision, both user-approved and both overturned by measurement, I told the user to weigh the third accordingly and wrote the same caveat into the research file beside the surviving option. A recommender's reliability is evidence the decision-maker needs, and withholding it is a quiet form of overclaiming.
- Disclose a contradiction between your own artifacts rather than letting a careful reader find it. The research file's §2 reported 9 clusters at modularity 0.4469 and §3 reported 10 at 0.4331 for the same corpus and seed, because one clustered the weighted graph and the other the simplified graph the null model requires. Writing the scope limitation explicitly, including which claim does NOT transfer, preserves credibility for the sections that are solid.
- `/dsm-research-add` assumes five numbered sub-tables in `dsm-docs/research/README.md`; this repo's README has a single `File | Purpose` table and is stale, omitting every research file added since Epoch 2. The instruction "sub-table 2" was unfollowable. Matched the file's actual format and flagged the divergence rather than restructuring, since restructuring is a separate decision.
- When a compressed reply has several plausible reads, check whether they converge on the same next action before asking for clarification. S56's two-word "Suggested work items" had three readings (elaborate / proceed / topic-select), but item 1 was gated on decisions only the user could make, so every reading produced the same correct next move, presenting that gate. State the read, act on the convergence, do not spend a turn on a bare "which one?". Extends S55 #117 (restate every compressed reply) and S54 #97 (gate on the cost of a misread) with the convergence test.
- A hedge word in an approval is a scope limit, honor it literally. "My lean: D" was read as direction-setting and NOT as authorization to launch an EXP-011-shaped run (24 agents, ~644K subagent tokens); "support the research if necessary with online resources" bounded external delegation to questions the internal pass could not answer; "i am not sure" was weighed as evidence against the agent's own third recommendation. The user's qualifiers are the cheapest available signal about how far an approval reaches.
- An IDE file-open is ambient context, never an instruction. Mid-problem the user opened DEC-009, the constraint sitting directly under the coverage question; the agent read it and explicitly refused to infer a request to reopen the decision. That restraint was load-bearing, because the research then found DEC-009's revisit clause newly satisfiable, and an inferred instruction would have contaminated that finding. Use the signal to inform what you read, not to infer what the user wants decided.
- Narrowing your own approved proposal is the safe direction, and still gets reported with its residual risk and mitigation. Having proposed a boot commit of 5 files, the agent excluded the live session transcript (mid-session, it belongs to the wrap-up commit), flagged the narrowing rather than folding it in, named the residual risk (the transcript could bundle into a later content commit) and pre-committed to the mitigation (pathspec commits all session, which held). Inverse case of S55 #123, which governs widening.
- Before spending a pre-registered gate, ask which decisions each possible outcome would change. The agent had recommended running EXP-012 immediately on the surviving design and reversed itself on the user's hesitation: even a clean PASS would leave the blocking problem (25% coverage) untouched, so the sprint's one gate would have graded a sub-question. "Running an experiment that cannot change the decision is theatre." Check outcome-to-decision coupling before checking cost or availability.
- Record your own read BEFORE a commissioned independent source lands, so later agreement is verifiable as independent. The agent wrote down that the vision doc's connectivity vocabulary is hubs/orphans/hotspots rather than clustering, explicitly noting it was on record before the adversarial agent reported; that agent then independently found Aider chose personalized PageRank on the same problem shape. Convergence from a timestamped prior read is evidence; convergence noticed after reading the report is unfalsifiable.
- The checkable prescriptions in a subagent report are its highest-value content, run them rather than cite them, and treat two independently commissioned agents prescribing the SAME test as the signal to run it. Both S56 external agents independently prescribed a degree-preserving null model; running it produced the session's decisive number (2.8% modularity excess) and invalidated the agent's own quality metric. Two further claims from those reports were verified locally (the partition type actually in use, PageRank availability) instead of being repeated on authority. Extends S52 #66 from cross-model review to commissioned research.
- Audit your own contamination before designing an answer key, and resolve an ambiguous success criterion BEFORE the run. The agent had proposed the surviving design, proposed running the gate, and already published a favourable qualitative read of its output, so any key written afterwards would be one the design passes; it pre-registered, sought user approval of the key so the standard was not its own, and halted on the P4 gate's "cuts across obvious boundaries" wording, whose two readings give opposite verdicts and cannot be chosen post-hoc without motivated reasoning. Extends S53 #82 (pre-register criteria) with the stake-audit and the ambiguity-first rule.
- In chunked drafting, escalate a thrice-repeated disclosure into a decision request, and offer a protocol deviation as its own micro-gate. Three consecutive bites overran their Gate 2 budgets (640 vs 400, 525 vs 350, 942 vs 700 words); at the third the agent stopped flagging per-section and surfaced the systematic ~30% underestimate with two options, and the user released the budget. Separately it declined to fold a short adjacent section into a bite unilaterally and instead offered the combined bite as a proposed deviation, which was approved. Gate 2 section budgets need a ~30% upward calibration.
- A negative result only prevents re-spend if the falsification condition and its numbers live in the artifact rather than the transcript. The research file's elimination section was written so that re-proposing weighted CONTAINS requires confronting the pre-registered sweep first, and the sources section recorded what was consulted and deliberately NOT used with reasons, carried the gathering agents' evidence-quality flags into the list, and stated which claims the agent verified itself versus reported at the gathering agent's assigned confidence. Without the rejected set and the verification boundary, a later reader re-finds the discards and assumes they were missed.
